Growth Hormone causes Growth. In children this means Gigantism (in Adults it is called acromegaly). If there is a lack of growth hormone it will cause dwarfism.  The effects of growth hormone are mediated by IGF-1 which stands for Insulin like growth factor. It has a similar structure to insulin and is produced by the liver.  IGF-1 stimulates growth of cartilage and bones. This means that children who have excessive levels will grow to be very tall.  Excess growth hormone also increases glucose production in the liver. This leads to diabetic symptoms such as increased thirst, increased urination and weight loss.  Excess growth hormone also increases fat deposition in tissues. This gives them a 'moon face' appearance.  Excess growth hormone also causes a number of other problems including joint pain and carpal tunnel syndrome due to soft tissue enlargement. It may also affect fertility.  Excess growth hormone is usually caused by a tumour on the pituitary gland or hypothalamus which causes excess release of growth hormone releasing hormone.  There is no effective treatment for excess growth hormone in children. Treatment is aimed at controlling complications with medication. Surgery to remove the tumour is not recommended until the child has stopped growing.  Excess growth hormone in adults can be treated with surgical removal of the tumour or drugs. Serous otitis media is an infection of the space usually filled with air (the middle air) that lies between the eardrum and the inner ear. Serous otitis media occurs most commonly when mucus gets trapped in the Eustachian tube due to swelling from an upper respiratory infection such as a cold. The mucus then becomes infected and pus-like fluid begins to accumulate in the middle ear. This creates a favorable environment for bacteria to grow causing acute inflammation of the middle ear. Symptoms of serous otitis media may include hearing loss, fever, painful inflammation of the ear, itching, headache, swollen lymph nodes, and balance problems. Treatment depends on the severity of symptoms but may include antibiotics, steroids, myringotomy (piercing the tympanic membrane), and grommets (ventilation tubes placed in the eardrums). Sources: https://www.hear-it.org/serous-otitis-media-middle-ear-infection and http://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/154627.php#symptoms_of_serous_otitis_media Serous otitis is not the same as Otosclerosis which involves abnormal growth of skin in the middle ear. It also isn't temporary deafness experienced after exposure to loud noises (acoustic trauma), damage to cochlea hair cells due to the failure of cells that control K+ ion secretion to migrate into the tissue during development (otosclerocystesis), or ringing in the ears (tinnitus). Caffeine is a diuretic, it also causes vasoconstriction of peripheral vessels and relaxes smooth muscle. This is achieved by inhibiting the breakdown of cAMP which leads to activation of PKA. PKA phosphorylates serine/threonine in the myosin light chain. This allows more cross bridges to form between actin and myosin leading to increased contraction of cardiac muscle cells. Caffeine also acts as a positive inotrope and positive chronotrope. It does this by increasing the release of noradrenaline from the sympathetic nerve endings. Noradrenaline then binds to b2 adrenoceptors on cardiomyocytes. This results in the activation of adenylyl cyclase causing increased production of cAMP. Caffeine inhibits the breakdown of cAMP and thus it has the same effects as stated above. The increase in cAMP then leads to phosphorylation of L type calcium channels allowing more Ca+ to enter cardiomyocytes. This leads to increased calcium ion mediated excitability and hence an increased heart rate. It also leads to increased calcium ion calmodulin complexes which activate myosin light chain kinase which leads to increased force of contraction. Antibodies are a part of the adaptive immune response and they activate the classical pathway of the complement system. This leads to the formation of C3 convertase which eventually creates C3b which binds to the microbe/cell wall and triggers other complement proteins to stick there as well. This is called opsonisation. This makes it easier for phagocytes to recognise and eat the cell as there are now receptors on its surface. If the C3b also binds to membranes it can punch holes in them using enzymatic activity of MACHINE which forms the membrane attack complex. This is very dangerous to cells so this only happens in the case of infection e.g. bacterial or fungal infection. In normal tissue the C3b binds to regulatory proteins that stop the process. The alternative pathway of complement activation occurs all the time without any help from antibodies. It involves water breaking down unstable complex molecules spontaneously. This is important in the early stages of immunity before antibodies are produced against a pathogen. Mannan lectin is a protein that detects carbohydrates (specifically mannose) on invading microbes and triggers the lectin pathway of complement activation. Remember that there are three main functions of the complement system; opsonisation, inflammation and lysis. Opsonisation is when the complement proteins stick to the cell wall making it easier for phagocytes to engulf it. Inflammation is where the chemicals H2O2 and histamines are produced causing redness and swelling. Lysis is where the membrane attack complex forms and punches holes into the cell wall.
